characters: JESUS (never show his face: always from behind, hands only, a distant figure, or the scene around him): about 30, slim and sun-browned, shoulder-length dark brown wavy hair, undyed cream linen tunic, worn brick-red outer mantle, simple leather sandals. PETER: about 40, broad-shouldered fisherman, grey-streaked black curly hair, thick short beard, faded blue-grey tunic with a rope belt. JOHN THE BAPTIST: about 30, lean and wiry, long wild dark hair, untrimmed beard, rough brown camel-hair garment, wide leather belt. NICODEMUS: about 60, neatly trimmed silver beard, deep indigo robe, white prayer shawl with blue-fringed corners, carries a small clay oil lantern. JOSEPH OF ARIMATHEA (day 3 only): about 55, short grey beard, dark green robe. PHILIP: about 30, short black beard, sand-colored traveling tunic, leather shoulder bag, dusty from the road. THE ETHIOPIAN OFFICIAL: about 40, dark brown skin, shaved head, tall and dignified, white linen robe with a gold-embroidered collar, reads a long scroll; his chariot is painted deep green with bronze fittings, pulled by two chestnut horses, with one driver. THE SAMARITAN WOMAN: about 35, olive skin, rust-red dress, dark brown head covering, a large terracotta water jar. KING JOSIAH: about 26, short black beard, thin gold circlet, royal purple robe. HILKIAH THE PRIEST: about 70, long white beard, white linen priestly robe and white turban. SHAPHAN THE SCRIBE: about 45, grey beard, dark blue robe, a reed pen tucked in his sash. TODAY FAMILY (modern, recurring across all seven films): MAYA, 16, Black American, natural curls worn in a high puff, oversized sage-green hoodie, small gold cross necklace, white sneakers; ELI, her brother, 19, short fade, light beard, faded denim jacket over a black tee; GRACE, their mom, about 45, shoulder-length locs, mustard cardigan; GRANDMA RUTH, about 72, short silver hair, round tortoiseshell glasses, floral blouse, carries a well-worn black leather Bible with soft pages; DANIEL, Maya's friend, 17, Korean American, black hair with a middle part, cream varsity jacket.

1.story: The Last Supper, Luke 22:14-23 with 1 Corinthians 11:23-25 (Mark 14:12-25)
1.point: Communion means sharing: Christians share bread and cup because Jesus asked his friends to remember him with that meal on the night before he died.
1.script: The night before he died, Jesus shared a Passover dinner with his friends, in a borrowed upstairs room. He knew what was coming. He knew one friend at that table would hand him over. He took the bread anyway. He gave thanks. He broke it. And he passed it around, even to that friend. This is my body. Then the cup. And one request: this do in remembrance of me. Christians call it communion. It means sharing: one loaf, many people. And for many Christians, remembering means more than a memory. That night is present again. So when that tray comes down the row at church, it's carrying more than bread. It's carrying a dinner that never ended.
pictures: Picture 1: A small upstairs room in old Jerusalem at night, whitewashed stone walls, oil lamps glowing on a low wooden table set with flatbread, bowls and a clay cup. Twelve friends recline on cushions around it, Peter and others in warm lamplight. Jesus sits at the center, seen only from behind: shoulder-length dark brown hair, cream tunic, brick-red mantle. Wide shot, warm amber light, deep blue night through a small window.

Picture 2: The far end of the same table. One friend sits slightly apart, his face half in shadow, a small leather coin pouch at his belt, eyes lowered. In the soft-focus foreground, the shoulder and brick-red mantle of Jesus, seen from behind. Tense, quiet mood, single lamp flame between them.

Picture 3: Close-up of a man's hands (Jesus, sleeve of the cream tunic visible) holding a round flatbread over the table, mid-break, small crumbs falling, lamplight glowing on the bread. No face. Rich, reverent, painterly.

Picture 4: Pieces of broken bread being passed hand to hand along the table, one hand to the next, ending at the shadowed friend from picture 2, whose hand reaches out to take it. Low angle along the tabletop, lamps in the background.
Picture 5: A simple clay cup of dark wine lifted in two hands above the table, lamplight catching the rim, the friends' faces softly blurred and watching. No face of Jesus; only hands and sleeves.

Picture 6: TODAY. A bright modern church on a Sunday morning, rows of chairs. A silver tray of tiny cups is being passed down the row. Maya, 16, in her sage-green hoodie, holds a tiny cup and waits, Grandma Ruth beside her with her soft-paged Bible on her lap, Eli on the other side passing the tray along. Warm window light, relaxed and real, not posed.
motion: Slow push-in across the table toward the figure seen from behind while the lamp flames flicker.
The camera holds still as the shadowed friend slowly lowers his eyes and the lamp flame wavers between them.
Close and steady as the hands pull the bread apart and crumbs drift down in the lamplight.
Gentle sideways track along the tabletop following the bread from hand to hand until the last hand takes it.
The cup rises slowly into the light while the camera tilts up with it; background faces stay soft.
Slow drift along the row as the tray moves from hand to hand and Maya looks down at the tiny cup.

2.story: The baptism of Jesus in the Jordan, Mark 1:9-11 (with Matthew 28:19 and 1 John 4:8)
2.point: Christians believe in one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three persons and still one God, and they see love at the center of who God is.
2.script: A crowd stood in the Jordan River, waiting their turn. A wild preacher named John was baptizing people in its water. Then a carpenter from Nazareth waded in. Jesus. John baptized him. And as he came up out of the water, the sky tore open. The Spirit came down on him like a dove. And a voice from heaven said: You are my beloved Son. One river. One moment. All three. The Son in the water. The Spirit coming down. The Father's voice. Christians call it the Trinity. One God, three persons. Not three gods. The Bible says God is love, and love needs someone to love. So at the center of God, Christians see a relationship. Three, and still one.

open.text: the sky *tore open* over a river.

2.drop: And as he came up out of the water
beats: A crowd stood in the Jordan
The Bible says God is love
pictures: Picture 1: The Jordan River at mid-morning, green reeds and dry hills. A line of ordinary people in simple robes stands in the shallows waiting. Waist-deep in the river, John the Baptist in his rough camel-hair garment and leather belt, wild dark hair, lowers a man into the water. Wide shot, golden light, river glittering.

Picture 2: A lone figure wading into the river from the bank, seen from behind: shoulder-length dark brown hair, cream tunic, the brick-red mantle left folded on a rock on the shore. The crowd turns to watch. Camera low behind him at the water line.

Picture 3: Seen from behind and slightly above: the figure of Jesus rising up out of the water, back and shoulders streaming with water, John's hands on his shoulders. A spray of bright droplets catches the sun. No face visible.

Picture 4: The sky above the river splitting open: clouds parting in a great seam of gold-white light, and a pure white dove gliding down through the beam. Below, tiny in the frame, the river and the distant figure from behind. No figure of God anywhere; only light and sky.

Picture 5: A wide, quiet composition from the far bank: the ripples spreading on the water around the distant figure, the white dove just above him, a column of soft light falling from the opened sky. The crowd on the shore looks up in awe. Three elements clearly readable: water, dove, light.

Picture 6: TODAY. Outside a church on a sunny Sunday after the service. Grandma Ruth in her floral blouse pulls Maya, 16, into a big laughing hug, Eli, 19, wraps his arms around both of them, and Grace, their mom, laughs beside them. Warm, close, everyday family love.

The camera follows low behind the figure as he wades forward and the water ripples out around him.

The clouds slowly pull apart and the light widens as the dove glides down through the beam.
Very slow pull-back from the river as the ripples spread and the light settles.
Gentle handheld drift around the family hug as they laugh and sway.

3.story: Nicodemus comes to Jesus at night, John 3:1-8 (and John 19:38-42)
3.point: Born again, in Jesus's word anothen, also means born from above: a new start that comes from God's Spirit as a gift, and no one is too old for it.
3.script: Night in Jerusalem. A respected teacher named Nicodemus slipped through the dark streets to find Jesus. Maybe he didn't want to be seen. Jesus told him: no one can see the kingdom of God unless they're born again. Nicodemus didn't get it. How can a man be born when he is old? Climb back into his mother? But the word Jesus used has two meanings. Again. And from above. A new birth from God's Spirit, like the wind. You hear it, but you can't see where it comes from. Nicodemus left with questions. The next time we see him, he isn't hiding. He's carrying spices to bury Jesus. Nobody gives birth to themselves. It's a gift. And you're never too old to start again.

open.text: a famous teacher sneaks out at *night.*

3.drop: But the word Jesus used has two meanings.
beats: A new birth from God's Spirit
The next time we see him
pictures: Picture 1: Jerusalem at night, a narrow stone alley between flat-roofed houses under a deep blue sky full of stars. Nicodemus, about 60, silver beard, deep indigo robe and blue-fringed white prayer shawl, walks quickly, glancing over his shoulder, a small clay lantern in his hand casting a warm circle of light.

Picture 2: A flat rooftop at night with a low wall and potted herbs. Nicodemus sits on a mat facing Jesus, who is seen only from behind: dark brown hair, brick-red mantle. The lantern sits on the floor between them. Over the shoulder of Jesus we see Nicodemus leaning in, listening hard.
Picture 3: Close on Nicodemus by lantern light, brow furrowed, hands spread open in a puzzled question, half a smile of disbelief. The edge of Jesus's mantle visible at the frame's edge.

Picture 4: A gust of night wind sweeps across the rooftop: the lantern flame bends sideways, the olive trees in the courtyard below toss, Nicodemus's prayer shawl lifts and its fringes fly. Nothing to see of the wind itself except what it moves. Seen from a little distance, Jesus from behind.

Picture 5: Evening in a quiet garden outside the city with a rock-cut tomb. Nicodemus, in the open now, carries a large clay jar of spices in both arms, walking beside Joseph of Arimathea in his dark green robe. Soft orange sunset light, still and respectful. No body shown.

Picture 6: TODAY. A front porch at night, string lights overhead, a warm breeze moving the trees. Eli, 19, in his denim jacket, and Grandma Ruth, 72, sit side by side on the steps, her soft-paged Bible open on her knees, both laughing at something. Cozy, real, unhurried.
motion: Slow tracking shot following Nicodemus down the alley as his lantern light swings on the walls.
Gentle push-in over the shoulder of the figure seen from behind toward Nicodemus's listening face.
Nicodemus slowly opens his hands wider; the camera holds close and the lantern glow flickers.
The wind gusts: the flame bends, the shawl lifts, the trees toss, and the camera holds steady.
Slow sideways track alongside the two men walking through the garden in the fading light.
Soft drift toward the steps as the string lights sway in the breeze and the two laugh.

4.story: Philip and the Ethiopian official, Acts 8:26-39 (with Romans 6:3-4)
4.point: Baptism comes from the Greek for dip or plunge: going under the water and coming up is the picture of a burial and a rising, the way Christians are welcomed in.
4.script: A desert road south of Jerusalem. A chariot rolling home to Ethiopia. Inside, a powerful official, treasurer to the queen, reading a scroll. He doesn't understand it. A man named Philip runs up beside the chariot. Do you understand what you're reading? How can I, unless someone guides me? So Philip climbs in and tells him about Jesus. Then, on that dry road, they pass water. Look, the official says, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized? He stops the chariot. They go down into the water together. Baptism comes from the Greek for dip, or plunge. Down, like a burial. Up, like rising to new life. Baby in a white gown, or sixteen in a pool: under the water, up again.

open.text: baptized on the side of a *desert road.*

4.drop: Then, on that dry road, they pass water.
pictures: Picture 1: A long empty desert road through rocky tan hills under a huge blue sky. A deep-green chariot with bronze fittings, pulled by two chestnut horses and a driver, rolls along. In the back sits the Ethiopian official, shaved head, white linen robe with a gold-embroidered collar, reading a long unrolled scroll. Wide, sunlit, epic.

Picture 2: Philip, dusty sand-colored tunic, leather bag bouncing, running alongside the moving chariot, calling up to the official, who lowers his scroll and looks down with curiosity. Dust kicking up from wheels and sandals. Side-on action shot.

Picture 3: The chariot slowing near a small pool of clear water among palms and reeds in the desert, bright and surprising against the dry land. The official, now seated beside Philip, points at the water, excited. The open scroll rests across both their laps.

Picture 4: The chariot stopped, horses drinking at the edge. Philip and the official wade together into the pool, both robes darkening with water, the official's face calm and joyful. The driver watches from beside the horses. Midday light glittering on the surface.

Picture 5: The official coming up out of the water, head back, water streaming from his face and shoulders, eyes closed, mouth open in a breath of joy, Philip's hand on his shoulder. Bright spray against the blue sky. No blood, pure light and water.

Picture 6: TODAY. An indoor church baptism pool lit warm and blue. Maya, 16, in a white T-shirt, is coming up out of the water, laughing and wiping her eyes, held by a pastor's arm. On the edge, Grace, Eli and Grandma Ruth cheer and clap; Daniel films on his phone. Joyful, real, everyday.

The camera tracks sideways with Philip running as the chariot rolls and dust rises.
Slow push toward the pool as the chariot slows and the palm fronds sway.
The camera holds wide as the two men wade in and gentle ripples spread out across the pool.
Slow-motion rise from the water with spray catching the sun; the camera tilts up slightly.
Handheld push toward the pool edge as Maya comes up and the family claps.

5.story: The woman at the well in Samaria, John 4:5-42
5.point: A testimony is a witness statement, from the Greek martys, a witness: saying plainly what happened to you, which is how a whole town first heard about Jesus.
5.script: Noon. The hottest hour. A woman walks alone to a well outside her town in Samaria, a heavy jar on her shoulder. A tired traveler is sitting there. A Jewish man. Jesus. He asks her for a drink. She's stunned. Jews and Samaritans didn't mix. They talk, and he tells her her own story, everything she'd ever done. She leaves her water jar behind and runs into town. Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. And the Gospel says many believed because of her testimony. Testimony comes from the Greek for witness: someone who says what they saw. Not a sales pitch. Not a performance. Just: here's what happened to me. Your story counts too. Even a quiet one.

open.text: she dropped everything to be a *witness.*

5.drop: She leaves her water jar behind
beats: He asks her for a drink
pictures: Picture 1: Blazing noon sun over dry hills in Samaria, a high mountain in the distance. A dirt path leads to an old stone well. The Samaritan woman, rust-red dress, dark brown head covering, walks alone toward it with a large terracotta jar on her shoulder, her shadow short beneath her. Bleached, hot light.

Picture 2: At the well, a weary traveler sits on the stone rim, seen only from behind: dusty sandals, cream tunic, brick-red mantle loosened, dark brown hair. The woman stops a few steps away, jar on her shoulder, surprised and wary.

Picture 3: Over the shoulder of Jesus, seen from behind: the woman lowering the rope and wooden bucket into the well, water sloshing, her face caught mid-reaction, eyebrows raised, half-guarded, half-curious. The conversation feels alive.

Picture 4: The terracotta jar left standing alone on the rim of the well, water still dripping from it. In the background, small on the bright path, the woman in her rust-red dress running back toward the town, her head covering flying. Jesus, from behind, sits watching.

Picture 5: The town gate of a small stone village. The woman, breathless, points back toward the well while a crowd of villagers, old men, mothers with children, young workers, pours out of the gate after her, curious. Late-afternoon gold light.

Picture 6: TODAY. A youth-group bonfire at night by a lake, sparks rising. Away from the big circle, Maya, 16, sits on a log with Daniel, 17, in his varsity jacket, telling him something quietly, hands around a paper cup of cocoa; he listens closely. Eli laughs with friends in the background. Warm firelight, honest and unforced.

Slow push-in past the seated figure seen from behind toward the woman, who stops.
The bucket rope slides down as the camera holds over the shoulder and the woman's expression shifts.
Water drips from the jar in the foreground while the running woman grows smaller down the path.
Gentle pull-back from the gate as more villagers stream out behind her.
Slow drift toward the two on the log as sparks float up from the fire.

6.point: The Holy Spirit is the third name of the Trinity: in the Bible's old languages the same word means breath, wind and spirit, and Jesus called the Spirit the one called alongside you.
6.script: Fifty days after Passover. Jesus's friends were packed into one house. Weeks earlier, Peter had sworn three times he didn't even know Jesus. Then a sound came from the sky, like a rushing wind. It filled the whole house. Something like flames rested on each of them. They spilled into the street, speaking. Visitors from every nation heard them in their own languages. And Peter, the one who'd been afraid, stood up in front of the crowd and spoke. In the Bible's old languages, spirit, breath and wind are one word. Jesus called the Spirit the one called alongside you. In your corner, on the day you're scared to speak. The Spirit grows quiet things: love, joy, peace. Closer than your own breath.
6.drop: Then a sound came from the sky
pictures: Picture 1: An upstairs room in a Jerusalem house in early morning, crowded with Jesus's friends, men and women, sitting close on mats and benches, a few oil lamps still lit, pale dawn through a small window. Picture 4: A busy Jerusalem street in bright morning sun. The friends pour out of the doorway, faces lit up, talking with their hands. A crowd of visitors in clothing from many lands, striped Persian robes, Egyptian linen, North African wraps, turns toward them, amazed, each one hearing their own language.

Picture 5: Peter standing on stone steps above a huge crowd, one arm raised, speaking with fire and calm, the morning sun behind him. The crowd stretches into the street, listening. Low angle from within the crowd, looking up at him.

Picture 6: TODAY. Early morning in a car outside a high school. Maya, 16, in her sage-green hoodie, holding note cards for a class speech, closes her eyes and takes one slow breath. In the driver's seat, Grace, her mom, rests a hand on her shoulder and smiles. A soft breeze through the open window lifts Maya's curls.

7.story: King Josiah and the scroll found in the temple, 2 Kings 22:3-13 and 23:1-3 (with Genesis 2:9, Revelation 22:1-2)
7.point: The Bible is not one book but a library (ta biblia, the books) that Christians read as one story, from a garden with a tree of life to a city made new.
7.script: Jerusalem. The temple needed repairs, so a young king named Josiah sent in workers. Then, during the work, the high priest found something. An old scroll. The book of the law. A scribe read it out loud to the king. And Josiah tore his clothes. His people had stopped living by these words. So he gathered everyone, young and old, and had it read to all of them. The word Bible means the books. It's a library: poems, laws, letters, four lives of Jesus, written over centuries. And Christians read it as one story. It starts in a garden with a tree of life. On the last page, that tree is back, in a city made new. That library is on your phone right now.

open.text: a lost book, found in a *renovation.*

pictures: Picture 1: The ancient temple courtyard in Jerusalem under scaffolding of rough timber, workers carrying cut stone blocks and wooden beams, dust hanging in shafts of golden afternoon light. King Josiah, about 26, gold circlet, royal purple robe, watches from the steps with his advisers.

Picture 2: Inside a dim temple storeroom, broken pottery and dusty chests. Hilkiah the priest, long white beard, white linen robe and turban, kneels and lifts an old leather scroll out of the rubble, a single beam of light falling on it, dust floating in the air.

Picture 3: The royal hall. Shaphan the scribe, grey beard, dark blue robe, reads the unrolled scroll aloud. King Josiah, standing, grips the neck of his purple robe and tears it in grief, his face stricken. Advisers stare. Dramatic lamplight.

Picture 4: A vast crowd gathered in the temple courtyard, old men, mothers, children on shoulders, young workers, all listening, as the king stands on a raised platform and the scroll is read aloud to everyone. Morning light, wide epic shot.

Picture 5: A luminous split image without any text: on the left, a lush garden at dawn with a great fruit-laden tree of life; on the right, a radiant city of light with a clear river running through it and the same tree growing on its banks. The river seems to flow from one side to the other, joining them.

Picture 6: TODAY. A city bus in the morning. Maya, 16, in her sage-green hoodie, earbuds in, scrolls a Bible app on her phone, smiling slightly. Inset in the same warm scene through the bus window reflection: Grandma Ruth at her kitchen table at home with her soft-paged black leather Bible open, Eli leaning over her shoulder reading along. Warm, everyday, cool.

The camera holds as Josiah pulls at his robe and the lamp flames shiver.

sources_check: Day 1: Luke 22:14-23 (KJV 22:19 'this do in remembrance of me'); Mark 14:12-25; 1 Corinthians 11:23-25; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17
Day 2: Mark 1:9-11 ('You are my beloved Son', Mark 1:11); Matthew 28:19; 1 John 4:8; Tertullian, Against Praxeas 2-3; Augustine, On the Trinity 8
Day 3: John 3:1-8 (3:3 born again, 3:4 'How can a man be born when he is old?', 3:8 the wind); John 19:38-42 (Nicodemus brings spices)
Day 4: Acts 8:26-39 (8:31 'How can I, except some man should guide me?', 8:36 'here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?'); Romans 6:3-4; Liddell-Scott-Jones on baptizo
Day 5: John 4:5-42 (4:9 Jews and Samaritans, 4:29 'Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did', 4:39 believed because of the woman's testimony); Acts 1:8 (martys)
Day 6: Acts 2:1-41; Luke 22:54-62 (Peter's three denials); John 14:16, 26 (the Paraclete); Genesis 1:2 / John 20:22 (ruach, pneuma); Galatians 5:22-23
Day 7: 2 Kings 22:3-13 and 23:1-3; Genesis 2:9; Revelation 22:1-2; Liddell-Scott-Jones on ta biblia
risks: Day 1: 'he passed it around, even to that friend' follows Luke 22:21, where the betrayer is still at the table after the bread and cup; in John's account Judas leaves earlier, so some readers will say Judas did not receive the bread. 'That night is present again' is framed as 'for many Christians' because churches differ on real presence vs. memorial.
Day 1: the borrowed upstairs room is from Mark 14:14-15 (a guest room lent by a householder); fine, but worth a glance.

Day 2: 'The Father's voice' identifies the voice from heaven as the Father, which is the standard Christian reading but is an interpretation; the voice itself is depicted only as light, with no figure of God. 'All three in one moment' is a classic Trinitarian reading of the baptism scene, not a claim the text names the Trinity.

Day 3: 'Maybe he didn't want to be seen' is a common interpretation of why Nicodemus came at night, flagged with 'maybe'. Picture 5 places the burial at evening in a garden near the tomb (John 19:41-42); no body is shown.

Day 4: the official's quote is paraphrased from Acts 8:36-37 (verse 37 is missing from the oldest manuscripts and is not used). Calling him 'treasurer to the queen' follows 8:27 (Candace); the text also calls him a eunuch, which the film leaves out on purpose. Whether he went fully under is not stated, so pictures show wading in and coming up, which fits 'went down into the water' (8:38).

Day 5: 'Jews and Samaritans didn't mix' paraphrases John 4:9 ('have no dealings', or in some translations 'do not share things in common'). Noon is the 'sixth hour' (4:6) in the usual reckoning; 'walks alone' and any idea that she was shunned are interpretation, so the script avoids saying she was an outcast and leaves out her marriages entirely.

Day 6: the flames are 'like as of fire' (Acts 2:3) and painted as soft glowing light; speaking in tongues is described only as Acts 2 tells it (understood languages) because churches differ on tongues today. 'In front of the crowd' avoids claiming a number; 3,000 were baptized (2:41).

Day 7: identifying the found scroll (often linked with Deuteronomy) is left open on purpose. 'His people had stopped living by these words' paraphrases 2 Kings 22:13. Protestant/Catholic/Orthodox book counts are left out of the film (they are in the lesson) to keep it short.
All days: Jesus is never shown face-on (from behind, hands, or distant only); God is shown only as light and sky; the today family is the same fictional cast across all seven films.
